title: Lovable Cloud Automation: How to Set It Up (2026)
summary: Lovable cloud automation offers three plans: Free for testing, Pro when credits run out, Business for team administration needs.
body_markdown:
## Setting up Lovable Cloud automation in five stages


If the limits fit your job, the build is five stages, and each one leaves something working, so a failure points at the stage you just finished and nothing earlier. Run them in order, even though you'll want to skip ahead to the schedule.


### Stage 1: Enable Cloud and confirm the backend is live


Open your project, go to the Cloud tab and enable Cloud if it isn't already on. Lovable's button labels move between releases, so go by what the tab shows rather than a remembered name.


You're done when the tab lists a database and functions area with no setup prompt.


Open the database view and confirm you can see tables. If you can't, stop here, because everything after this depends on it.


Stage 2 is a function that writes one row. Start with a function that does almost nothing, so the first failure isn't buried in business logic. In the chat, ask for it in plain words:


> Create a backend function called` log_run` that inserts one row into a new table` automation_runs` with a timestamp and a status of "ok". Add a button on the dashboard that calls it.


Click the button once. You now have a working function, even though it does nothing useful yet.


### Stage 3: Add secrets for outside API keys


Add secrets only when the function needs to call something outside the app, such as an email service, a payment provider or an AI model. Ask Lovable to add the secret, then enter the value in the secure field it opens, never in the chat.


Name it in capitals, for example` EMAIL_API_KEY` , and have the function read it from its environment.


**Anything pasted into a prompt or written into code is exposed, so rotate any key that lands there.** I haven't confirmed where the Cloud tab lists saved secrets afterwards, so check that screen in your own project.


### Stage 4: Run it on a schedule or a webhook


Now the function gets its trigger, either a schedule or a webhook. Run` log_run` every morning at 8:00 and record each run in` automation_runs` , meaning you capture system state before the day's work begins.


For an event-driven job, ask for a webhook endpoint that calls the function when an outside service posts to it. Whether a given schedule granularity is allowed on your plan isn't something I can state, so check your plan's limits before promising customers a frequency.


### Stage 5: Test it and read the logs


Trigger the function by hand, then open its logs from the Cloud tab. A good run shows your insert and no error. Now open` automation_runs` and confirm a new row with the right timestamp. That row is the proof.


When the scheduled time passes, confirm a second row appeared without you touching anything. If it didn't, the logs will say whether the trigger never fired or the function failed after it did.
